content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper addresses handwriting recognition from ballpoint pens fitted with sensors, i.e., online handwriting (OnHW) recognition. This is a novel field and got a lot of interest in the recent years. content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths:**
- The proposed models outperform state-of-the-art results by Ott et al. (2020; 2022a) by 11.3% to 23.56% and by 2.17% to 4.34% for ML and DL models, respectively. Using an ensemble learning method, results are further improved about 3.08% to 7.01%.
- The authors focus further on the explainability of results for the different models, which is highly interesting for many applications based on multivariate time series classification.
- The authors provide a large search of hyperparameters for different DL models.
- The list of references seems to be complete.

**Weaknesses:**
- The paper does not propose a contribution that is of broader interest to the ICLR community. It proposes architectural optimizations (engineered), an ensemble learning strategy known from literature (voting), and known explainability methods (e.g. LIME) to an handwriting recognition dataset. There is no general insight or benefit that goes beyond of the scope of the work from Ott et al. and the OnHW dataset
The paper is easy understandable, but the writing could be improved at some points.

**Some detailed points:**
- The abbreviation MTS for multivariate time series is not introduced by used in Section 4.2.1.
- Please indicate in Figure 2 the kind of the sensor data and the orientation (x, y, or z) for each of the 13 channels. Furthermore, add an explanation for the colors green and red in Figure 2.
- Why have the characters in Figure 3 different lengths of approx. 105 and approx. 110?
- Use \citep instead of \cite that makes reading easier: For example, instead of
“Handwriting is defined to be the writing characteristics of an individual Priya et al. (2016).”
use “Handwriting is defined to be the writing characteristics of an individual (Priya et al., 2016).”
- The force is not available as binary value (written on page 2), but as a float value between 0 (no force) and 4,096 (maximal force).
- The paper often reads a bit like a “story on the way” where also some explored dead ends are being described. It would be much better for the paper to write the storyline differently (e.g., don’t explain plurality voting and then state why it’s worse than weighted voting or soft voting. Instead explain the best method and afterwards drop some words to discuss those alternative approaches and why you didn’t choose them – or even omit that discussion at all).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity:** The Methods and results are clearly described.

**Quality:** The quality of writing can be improved at points. The technical quality is good.

**Novelty:** The paper proposes improved results and an explainability of models for online handwriting recognition but the paper lacks novelty with respect to technical contribution to ICLR.

**Reproducibility:** The authors provide a repository with all models for reproducibility. This repository might be used for other datasets, also.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper addresses the novel field of online handwriting recognition (i.e., time-series classification). The authors provide a large variety of ML and DL methods and significantly improve state-of-the-art results and provide a well-explained analysis why models outperform others. However, there are not technical contributions to the ICLR community.

The paper is a nice piece of engineering work that improves handwriting recognition proposed in earlier work on a known dataset. However, it does not go beyond that (neither in data sets nor in baseline applications). Hence, the work is not a good fit to ICLR. I suggest the authors to look for a more proper venue for their work, e.g., UbiComp, IMWUT, IJDAR, etc.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The manuscript presents a bag of traditional ML and state-of-the-art DL methods on online handwriting dataset to classify lowercase and uppercase characters. The reported accuracy improvement is up to 23.56% for ML models and up to 7.01% for DL models. A list of ensemble methods are presented to combine different classifiers to further improve the results (up to 2.98% over the proposed DL models). Some explanations of why ensemble works is also provided.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 
- The paper presents an application of very well known methods (both traditional ML approaches like Dynamic Time Warping, SVM, RBF, KNN and later DL approaches like LSTM-FCN, ResCNN, ResNet, XceptionTime etc.) to improve accuracy of online handwriting character recognition. 
- In particular, its contribution is pre-processing of the data, and extracting statistical features using a published approach called tsfresh software (that is more of a blackbox to the authors it appears)
- A loaded encoded representations of the models would be provided along with the DL models to the public for evaluation and research

Weakness
- The paper tries to solve a well known problem using an already published feature extraction (aka 'preprocessing') followed by known ML and DL methods. This is followed by pretty outdated ensemble methods to combine the approaches. It is hard to find novelty in the paper.
- Using a mean and variance metric, 'outlier' data instances were discarded making the dataset purportedly more uniform, and hence easier to solve. Those outliers are the hard job, especially in problems like online handwriting character recognition, where accuracies otherwise tend to run in above 90s.
- The only novelty in the paper, the feature extraction aka preprocessing step, seems to be a blackbox tfresh software, whose details are obscure to the best
- The basic understanding of pattern recognition is lacking. In page 4, it is stated that each feature should be able to predict any of the 26 classes! If that were true, only 1 feature would have suffice. It is not expected that one or even a few features (especially for DL methods) would be enough to classify N classes.
- The other proposed contribution of the paper - ensemble methods, are well known methods over 2 decades, with well known short comings. Nothing new is discovered in the paper.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper lacks a solid understanding of prior art, and fundamentals of machine learning and deep learning. While the authors promise the models availability to the general public for reproducibility, the details of them are absent in the paper. None of the proposed approaches - the filtering, preprocessing, ML or DL methods, ensemble methods are novel. The problem dataset itself is a toy dataset with individual online characters as separate classes. Furthermore, outliers and lefthandedness were not taken into account to add variability to the dataset. The overall writing is repetitive and abstract.

- Section 4.2.3: Not clear why a weight of 45 is chosen for top tier. As per the explanation, 4 classifiers * 9 weight for bottom tier would stil get to 36, so a weight of 37 for top tier would have sufficed
- Why were left-handed writers excluded from the dataset? Those writers, in particular, add variability that is hard to generalize
- What do the channels actually represent? The Figures 2 & 3 do not add explainability if the understanding of the channels is not provided. 
P1, last para: offline hw is produced 'after' the time of writing, not 'at'
content.summary_of_the_review:
- The paper tries to solve a well known problem using an already published feature extraction (aka 'preprocessing') followed by known ML and DL methods. This is followed by pretty outdated ensemble methods to combine the approaches. It is hard to find novelty in the paper. 
- None of the solutions are explained, rather used as black-boxes on a toy dataset
- The problem dataset itself is a toy dataset with individual online characters as separate classes. Furthermore, outliers and lefthandedness were not taken into account to add variability to the dataset. 
- The overall writing is repetitive and abstract. 
- The paper lacks a solid understanding of prior art, and fundamentals of machine learning and deep learning. 
- Experiments lack any description of visual examples of data, the challenges, and ablation studies. The provided explanations of failures are at human non-readable features, making it hard to understand what they are, and why a few work and others don't.
- While the authors promise the models availability to the general public for reproducibility, the details of them are absent in the paper.

If that were true, only 1 feature would have suffice. It is not expected that one or even a few features (especially for DL methods) would be enough to classify N classes.

$\textbf{- Noted}$

•	The other proposed contribution of the paper - ensemble methods, are well known methods over 2 decades, with well known short comings. Nothing new is discovered in the paper.

Clarity, Quality, Novelty And Reproducibility:

$\textbf{- As mentioned, the middle tier weights being 9 would sum to 36,}$
$\textbf{ so including the bottom tier, where there are 8 models each with a}$
$\textbf{ weight of 1, sums to 44.}$

•	Why were left-handed writers excluded from the dataset? Those writers, in particular, add variability that is hard to generalize

$\textbf{- The OnHW dataset did not have left-hand writers included.}$
$\textbf{ We agree that we would like to experiment with the inclusion}$
$\textbf{ of left-handed writers when made available to do so.}$

•	What do the channels actually represent? The Figures 2 & 3 do not add explainability if the understanding of the channels is not provided. P1, last para: offline hw is produced 'after' the time of writing, not 'at'

$\textbf{- Thank you, noted}$

•	The paper tries to solve a well known problem using an already published feature extraction (aka 'preprocessing') followed by known ML and DL methods. This is followed by pretty outdated ensemble methods to combine the approaches. It is hard to find novelty in the paper.

•	None of the solutions are explained, rather used as black-boxes on a toy dataset

•	The problem dataset itself is a toy dataset with individual online characters as separate classes. Furthermore, outliers and lefthandedness were not taken into account to add variability to the dataset.

$\textbf{- Noted above}$

•	The overall writing is repetitive and abstract.

•	The paper lacks a solid understanding of prior art, and fundamentals of machine learning and deep learning.

•	Experiments lack any description of visual examples of data, the challenges, and ablation studies. The provided explanations of failures are at human non-readable features, making it hard to understand what they are, and why a few work and others don't.

$\textbf{ Thank you for your comments, we will do our best to improve}$
$\textbf{ the paper}$

•	While the authors promise the models availability to the general public for reproducibility, the details of them are absent in the paper.

$\textbf{- As per the rules outlined by ICLR to keep submissions}$
$\textbf{ anonymous, we were not able to provide the code, however}$

$\textbf{ a higher tier of model outweighs all lower tier models together.}$
$\textbf{ This is further detailed in Section 4.2.3. The goal with the}$
$\textbf{ ensemble learning was to show that within the online}$
$\textbf{ handwriting space, we can improve upon existing singleton}$
$\textbf{ models, using this method.}$



$\textbf{-   Machine learning has been used to get results in previous}$
$\textbf{ online handwriting papers. We wanted to improve upon}$
$\textbf{ these results while keeping the models lightweight. This}$
$\textbf{ was included to complement the end-to-end deep learning}$
$\textbf{ models and ensemble models included in the results.}$

$\textbf{-  Tsfresh’s feature extraction method is the main reason}$
$\textbf{ behind our over 20\\% improvements in comparison to existing}$
$\textbf{ ML models. However, our DL-models do not use tsfresh}$
$\textbf{ whence they do learn from raw-signals with much improved}$
$\textbf{ results.}$

$\textbf{-  Thank you for your comment}$
